story: Texas State University is in the second phase of a TxDOT funded project that reads pavement damage out of paired 2D surface images and 3D depth data at pixel level. A pavement condition score is what TxDOT uses to identify roads needing repair and to plan the money for it. The score used to be set by a rater measuring distress by hand on a sampled portion of the road. The judgement is moving, and the same team's own paper says a pavement engineer still has to verify what the machine returns.
absence_method: One absence is carried, on frame 9, and it is scoped to the university's own release: the release attaches no date to any of the three next steps it names. Where the deck names a dated public room it is the Texas Transportation Commission's own calendar, and the copy says what that meeting is and never implies this project is on its agenda.

claims.text: Texas State University's news office reported on August 24th, 2026 that the project titled Artificial Intelligence for Pavement Condition Assessment from 2D/3D Surface Images has entered a second phase. The university describes that phase as closer to statewide deployment.

claims.verbatim_quote: is now in its second phase, closer to statewide deployment with faster, more precise pixel-level detection of pavement damage than manual inspections
claims.source_title: TXST Team Develops More Accurate Way to Evaluate Road Conditions
claims.note: Confirmed character for character on two independent fetches. The full sentence reads: The project, "Artificial Intelligence for Pavement Condition Assessment from 2D/3D Surface Images," is now in its second phase, closer to statewide deployment with faster, more precise pixel-level detection of pavement damage than manual inspections.

claims.text: The method pairs ordinary photographs with depth data so the system can separate real damage from stains and rank severe hazards above minor cracking.

claims.verbatim_quote: By pairing 2D photos with 3D depth maps, the system distinguishes real damage from stains, trace cracks, and prioritizes severe hazards like crumbling concrete over minor surface cracks.

rejected.finding: more than 428,000 vehicle interactions per year on Texas roads
rejected.reason: The string is genuinely on the page and was confirmed twice, so this is not a fetch failure. It is rejected on meaning. The release gives no definition of a vehicle interaction, no source and no unit that can be checked, and 428,000 per year across a statewide network is implausible on its face. Publishing it would put an unexplained and probably wrong number under this project's name.

The federal HM-60 tables in c12 and c13 are HTML and were used instead, but they count all public roads including local streets, so they do not answer what TxDOT itself maintains.
